title: Frequency arrays
overview: So far an array index has only been a position: `a[0]` is the first number, `a[1]` the second. Module 13 adds one new idea: use the **number itself as the index**. Make a counting array `f` filled with zeros. Whenever you read a number `x`, do `f[x]++`. After one loop, `f[x]` tells you how many times `x` appeared, with no searching. This is called a frequency array. If the idea still feels abstract, the worked examples below build it up slowly, with numbers, letters and a yes/no version.

concepts.explain: From the earlier modules you can read `n` numbers into an array with a loop, reach any element with `a[i]`, and count things with `cnt++`. Module 13 puts these together in a new way.

concepts.term: The new idea: the value is the index
concepts.explain: Until now you asked "which number is at position `i`?". A frequency array asks the other way round: "how many times did the number `x` show up?". The answer is kept in slot `f[x]`.

Input `1 2 3 4 5 3 2 1 5 3`. Start with `f` all zeros. Each number adds 1 to its own slot. At the end `f[1] = 2`, `f[2] = 2`, `f[3] = 3`, `f[4] = 1` and `f[5] = 2`. Print `f[1]` to `f[5]` and you have the answer.

concepts.term: Why not count with two loops?
concepts.explain: You could: for each `i` from 1 to M, walk the whole array and count the `i`s. But with N and M up to 100000 that is about 10^10 steps, far too slow for 1 second. The frequency array walks the numbers only once.
Every slot must start at 0 before you count. Inside `main`, write `int f[100005] = {0};`. An array declared above `main` (a global array) starts at zero on its own.
The biggest number you may see must still be a valid index. If numbers go up to 100000, `f[100000]` must exist, so declare at least 100001 slots.
Sometimes you only need to know whether `x` appeared. Then write `f[x] = 1` instead of `f[x]++`.
In Module 11, `c - '0'` turned a digit character into its value. In the same way `ch - 'a'` turns `a`..`z` into 0..25, so 26 slots can count lowercase letters.

files.title: Presence array with yes/no queries
files.what: Marks which numbers are in the array, prints the marks for 0 to 9, then answers queries asking whether a number is present.
steps: For each `a[i]`, set `freq[a[i]] = 1` to mark it as present.
Print `i` and `freq[i]` for `i` from 0 to 9, so you can see the marks.
Read `m` queries. For each `x`, print `YES` if `freq[x] == 1`, otherwise `NO`.
files.complexity: Time O(n + m) · Space O(max value)
files.output_note: The first 10 lines are `value mark`. Only 2, 3, 4 and 7 show `1`, and the repeated 4 is still just `1`. Then come the answers `4 YES`, `5 NO` and `7 YES`.
files.watch_out: A value of 100000 or more would write past the end of `freq`. Always check the limits before choosing the array size.

check.q: Why does 4 show 1 and not 2, even though it appears twice?
check.a: The code sets `freq[x] = 1` instead of adding 1, so it only records presence.

files.title: Frequency Array (count 1..M)
files.what: Counts how many times each number from 1 to M appears. This is the counting version of the frequency array.
steps: `int f[100000];` is global, so every slot starts at 0.
Read each number and do `f[a[i]] += 1` in the same loop.
Print `f[1]`, `f[2]`, and so on up to `f[m]`, one per line.
files.input_note: The sample from the statement: N = 10 numbers, each between 1 and M = 5.
files.output_note: Line i is how many times i appears: `2` (two 1s), `2` (two 2s), `3` (three 3s), `1` (one 4) and `2` (two 5s). This matches the expected output in the statement.
files.watch_out: The array `a` isn't really needed. You could read into a temporary `x` and do `f[x]++`.

check.q: If M were 6 with the same numbers, what would line 6 show?
check.a: `0`, because 6 never appears and a global array starts at zero.

files.title: Distinct letters in a string
files.what: Finds which lowercase letters appear in a fixed string and how many different letters there are. It uses a 26-slot presence array.
steps: The string is hard-coded as `"aaaaaagggggccjcc"`, and `f[26]` starts at zeros.
For each character, `ch - 'a'` gives its slot, and that slot is set to 1.
Loop over the 26 slots. Add each `f[i]` to `cnt`, and if `f[i]` is 1, print the letter `i + 'a'`.
Print `cnt`, the number of different letters.
files.output_note: `a 1`, `c 1`, `g 1` and `j 1` come out in alphabetical order, even though `g` comes before `c` in the string. The last line is `4`.
files.watch_out: Only lowercase letters are safe. An uppercase letter or a digit would give a negative index or one above 25.

check.q: Why do the letters come out sorted?
check.a: The second loop goes through the slots in order from 0 (`a`) to 25 (`z`), not in string order.

recap: A frequency array uses the number as the index: `f[x]` is about the number `x`.
`f[x]++` counts. `f[x] = 1` only marks that `x` was seen.
Fill it with zeros first, and make it bigger than the largest possible number.
One pass over the input is enough. There is no need to search the array again and again.
`ch - 'a'` turns a lowercase letter into an index from 0 to 25.
Printing `f` from the small end to the big end lists the values in sorted order.

check_yourself.q: After counting `2, 4, 3, 4, 5` into `f`, what are `f[4]` and `f[0]`?
check_yourself.a: `f[4]` is 2, because 4 came twice. `f[0]` is 0, because 0 never came.

check_yourself.q: What is the difference between `f[x]++` and `f[x] = 1`?
check_yourself.a: `f[x]++` counts how many times `x` came. `f[x] = 1` only remembers that `x` came at least once, so it stays 1 however many times `x` repeats.

check_yourself.q: In a letter-count array, which letter does index 7 belong to, and how would you print it?
The word `apple` is counted into `f[26]`. What is `f['p' - 'a']`?
Why would you not use a frequency array when the numbers can be as large as 10^9?
check_yourself.a: The array must have a box for the biggest number, so it would need a billion slots. That does not fit in memory.

check_yourself.q: You forgot to fill the array with zeros first. What can go wrong?
check_yourself.a: A local array starts with rubbish values, so the counts are added on top of nonsense and the output is wrong. Use `= {0}`, or declare the array above `main`.

walkthrough.heading: 1. Picture a row of empty boxes
body: Imagine a long shelf with boxes on it, and every box has a label: box 0, box 1, box 2, box 3 and so on. All the boxes start empty.

Now someone reads numbers out loud to you: `3, 1, 3, 2, 3`. Each time you hear a number, you put one stone in **the box with that label**. You hear 3, so one stone goes in box 3. You hear 1, one stone in box 1. You hear 3 again, so box 3 now has two stones.
At the end you do not have to remember the numbers at all. You just look at the boxes: box 1 has 1 stone, box 2 has 1 stone, box 3 has 3 stones. That is the whole idea of a frequency array.
In C the shelf is an array called `f`, the box label is the array index, and putting a stone in a box is `f[x]++`. `f` must start all zeros, because all the boxes start empty.
walkthrough.snippet:
int f[100005] = {0};   // the empty shelf
f[3]++;                // one stone in box 3

walkthrough.heading: 2. Example one: counting numbers, step by step
body: Take the sample from the Frequency Array problem: the numbers are `1 2 3 4 5 3 2 1 5 3` and we care about the numbers 1 to 5.
We read the numbers one by one, and after each number we only change **one** box, the box with that number's label. Here is the shelf after every step.

Read the last line and you have the answer: 1 came twice, 2 came twice, 3 came three times, 4 came once, 5 came twice. That is exactly what the problem asks you to print, so the loop at the end just prints `f[1]` to `f[5]`.
Notice how little work this was. We touched each number once, and we never went back to look at the earlier numbers again.

walkthrough.heading: 3. Example two: counting letters of a word
body: The same trick works for letters, and this is where it becomes really handy. A letter is not a number, so it cannot be an index by itself. But you already know from Module 11 that `c - '0'` turns a digit character into a number. Letters work the same way: `ch - 'a'` gives 0 for `a`, 1 for `b`, 2 for `c`, and so on up to 25 for `z`.

So 26 boxes are enough for the whole alphabet. Take the word `banana`. Walking through it: `b` puts a stone in box 1, `a` in box 0, `n` in box 13, `a` again in box 0, `n` again in box 13, `a` again in box 0.
The shelf now says: box 0 (`a`) has 3, box 1 (`b`) has 1, box 13 (`n`) has 2, everything else 0. So `banana` has three `a`s, one `b` and two `n`s.
To print the letters back, turn the index into a character again by adding `'a'`: index 13 plus `'a'` is `n`.

walkthrough.heading: 4. Example three: only "is it there or not"
body: Sometimes you do not need the count, only a yes or no. Say the numbers `2 4 3 4 7` came in, and then someone keeps asking you: is 4 there? is 5 there? is 7 there?

Here you can write `f[x] = 1` instead of `f[x]++`. The box now holds a flag, not a count: 1 means "this number came", 0 means "it never came". Note that the repeated 4 still leaves box 4 at 1, because setting it to 1 twice changes nothing.
After that, answering a question is one line: `if(f[x] == 1) printf("YES\n"); else printf("NO\n");`. You do not search anything. You just look in the box.
This is the first program on this page, `frequency_array.c`.
walkthrough.snippet:
f[x] = 1;                 // mark: x was seen
if(f[4] == 1) printf("YES\n");

walkthrough.heading: 5. Why is this useful?
body: **It saves a huge amount of work.** The obvious way to count how many times each number from 1 to M appears is two loops: pick a number, then walk the whole array counting it. With N and M both 100000 that is 100000 × 100000 = 10,000,000,000 steps. No computer finishes that in 1 second. The frequency array reads the numbers once and prints the answers once, so it is about 200000 steps. The same problem, but fast enough to pass.

**Many questions become one lookup.** Once the boxes are filled, "how many 7s?" is `f[7]`, and "did 7 ever come?" is `f[7] > 0`. Even a thousand such questions cost almost nothing, because each one is a single peek into a box.

**It answers a whole family of everyday questions.** Which number came the most times? Walk the boxes and keep the biggest. Which numbers came exactly once? Boxes holding 1. Did any number repeat? A box that goes above 1. How many different numbers came? Count the non-empty boxes. Do two words use exactly the same letters? Count the letters of both and compare the two 26-box shelves.

**It gives you sorted order for free.** The boxes sit in order of their labels, so printing from the small end to the big end prints the values sorted, even though you never sorted anything. That is why the distinct letters in the third program come out alphabetically and not in the order they appear in the string.

**When it does not work.** The box label is an array index, so the numbers must be small and not negative. If values can be up to 10^9 you would need a billion boxes, which will not fit in memory, and a negative number would be an invalid index and crash the program. In those cases you need a different tool, which comes later in the course.
